name: Mental Maths: 3-Digit × 2-Digit Multiplication — Core & Friendly Factors
description: A KaTeX-enabled deck for three-digit by two-digit multiplication. It develops reliable one-factor splitting, nearby-tens adjustments, friendly factors such as 25, 50, 75, 99, 101, 125, and 250, plus estimates, error checks, and method selection.
estimatedTime: 175–220 minutes for a first focused pass; then 10–20 minute review bursts

cards.term: 3-Digit × 2-Digit: What is the reliable default method?
cards.definition:
Split the two-digit multiplier into tens and ones.

$$
\begin{aligned}
347\times26 \\
&=347\times20+347\times6 \\
&=6940+2082 \\
&=9022
\end{aligned}
$$
This keeps the number of partial products low and works for every question.

cards.term: 3-Digit × 2-Digit: Why split the 2-digit factor rather than both factors?
cards.definition:
It usually gives only two main partial products.

$$
\begin{aligned}
428\times34 \\
&=428\times30+428\times4 \\
&=12840+1712 \\
&=14552
\end{aligned}
$$
Splitting both factors is valid, but often creates unnecessary working-memory load.

cards.term: 3-Digit × 2-Digit: How do you use a nearby tens multiple?
cards.definition:
Rewrite the two-digit factor as a friendly tens multiple plus or minus a small correction.

$$
\begin{aligned}
248\times39 \\
&=248\times40-248 \\
&=9920-248 \\
&=9672
\end{aligned}
$$

When the three-digit factor is divisible by 4 or easily split around a multiple of 4.

$$
\begin{aligned}
384\times25 \\
&=96\times100 \\
&=9600
\end{aligned}
$$

When the factor is even: halve it, then multiply by 100.

$$
\begin{aligned}
468\times50 \\
&=234\times100 \\
&=23400
\end{aligned}
$$

When a factor of 8 is visible.

$$
\begin{aligned}
384\times125 \\
&=48\times1000 \\
&=48000
\end{aligned}
$$

Use 99 = 100 − 1 and 101 = 100 + 1.

$$
\begin{aligned}
376\times99 \\
&=37600-376 \\
&=37224
\end{aligned}
$$
A product by 99 is just below the product by 100.

Round both factors to friendly values.

For 347 × 26, estimate 350 × 30 = 10500. The exact result 9022 is plausible because 26 is considerably below 30.

Do not perform long written multiplication in your head. Keep whole chunks.

$$
\begin{aligned}
586\times37 \\
&=586\times30+586\times7 \\
&=17580+4102 \\
&=21682
\end{aligned}
$$

cards.term: 3-Digit × 2-Digit: When should you not use a trick?
cards.definition:
For ordinary factors without a nearby base or friendly factor, use the core split.

$$
\begin{aligned}
463\times27 \\
&=463\times20+463\times7 \\
&=9260+3241 \\
&=12501
\end{aligned}
$$

Use \(25=\frac{100}{4}\).

$$
\begin{aligned}
384\times25 \\
&=96\times100 \\
&=9600
\end{aligned}
$$

Use 39 = 40 − 1.

$$
\begin{aligned}
248\times39 \\
&=9920-248 \\
&=9672
\end{aligned}
$$
Use estimation and a last-digit check. For 428 × 34, estimate 400 × 30 = 12000, and the last digit must come from 8 × 4 = 32, so it ends in 2. Exact answer: 14552.

cards.term: 3-Digit × 2-Digit: Can a last-digit check prove the whole answer?
cards.definition: No. It can eliminate many incorrect answers, but it checks only the final digit. Pair it with estimation.

cards.term: Which estimate is better for 463 × 27: 1200, 12000, or 120000?
cards.definition: Best estimate: 12000. 463 ≈ 500 and 27 ≈ 30, so the product is in the low tens of thousands.
No. 8 × 4 = 32, so the product must end in 2.

cards.term: True or false: Splitting the 2-digit multiplier always gives a valid product.
cards.definition: True. It follows from a(10b + c) = a · 10b + a · c.

cards.term: True or false: A nearby-base method is always faster than core splitting.
cards.definition: False. It only helps when the correction is small and easy.
